decisions.headline: Brazil's EWZ up 13% as Lula hands the finance ministry to a banker
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Stocks] Brazil's EWZ up 13% as Lula hands the finance ministry to a banker
Huge reversal in Brazilian markets started yesterday
Markets are pricing a Brazil without a fiscal crisis
The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF is up 13% in premarket trading after Lula named Bradesco chairman Luiz Carlos Trabuco Cappi as his finance minister for the term starting in January.
After Lula's surprise win in October, USD/BRL rose above 6.00 and was there as recently as Monday. Equity markets craashed after the surprise election result. The worry was simple, Lula (in his fourth term) campaigned on an even-harder shift to the left with debt near 83% of GDP.
Instead, this is a major pivot that suggests the fiscal picture will remain credible and some of Lula's promises won't be met.
The moves:
- USD/BRL is down nearly 4% today and touched 5.48. The pair opened the week at 5.95 and is on track for its biggest weekly fall of the year.
- The Ibovespa rose 6.07% yesterday to 176,800 on reports that Trabuco had been sounded out. That was its best day since October, and futures are up another 2.85% today.
- Long-dated swap rates are down more than 60 bps.
That's a powerful signal.
There's history here. In 2014 Dilma Rousseff reportedly offered Trabuco the same job. He turned it down and she went with Joaquim Levy, another Bradesco man. Levy lasted about a year before he was pushed out and replaced by Nelson Barbosa. So the market loves the name, but we will have to see how the marriage plays out.
Trabuco's job is a hard one. Analysts estimate the adjustment needed to get back to a primary surplus at more than R$80 billion. The PT's leadership in the lower house is already pushing back, and parts of the left say he's too market-friendly. Dario Durigan stays in the job until January and is already working on spending measures with Lula. Expect the first proposals to be judged against what the market now expects.
On the FX side, Brazil's carry is still among the best in the world, and the one thing holding the real back was fiscal credibility. Lula just bought some and there's a squeeze here as well with the market wrong-footed. But at 5.50 a lot of good news is priced in, and the real was at 4.88 in May before the election scare.
USD/BRL daily:
On the equity side, with the pre-market rally EWZ is trading at a trailing P/E of about 11.2x and a yield of 4.0%. Today's rally brings it back to virtually flat YTD.
Source URL: https://investinglive.com/stocks/brazil-s-ewz-up-13-as-lula-hands-the-finance-ministry-to-a-banker/

[ECB] Decisions taken by the Governing Council of the ECB (in addition to decisions setting interest rates)
Decisions taken by the Governing Council of the ECB (in addition to decisions setting interest rates)
November 2026
27 November 2026
External communication
Agreement for Sweden to join T2
On 25 November 2026 the ECB announced that it had concluded an agreement with Sveriges Riksbank for Sweden to join T2, the Eurosystem’s real-time gross settlement system. More information is available in the press release issued at the occasion of the signing ceremony with ECB President Christine Lagarde and Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen of the T2 currency participation agreement.
Market operations and market infrastructure and payments
Acceptance of marketable assets issued on distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime as Eurosystem collateral
On 19 November 2026 the Governing Council approved the acceptance of marketable assets issued on DLT platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime Regulation (EU) 2022/858 and reachable via TARGET2-Securities (T2S) as eligible collateral for Eurosystem credit operations, subject to specific Eurosystem requirements. This decision is part of a roadmap exploring ways to expand eligibility to assets issued and settled entirely on DLT networks. The decision is due to take effect in June 2027 and is explained in a press release available on the ECB’s website. It follows the ECB announcement of 27 January 2026 that marketable assets issued in central securities depositories using DLT will be accepted as collateral. These decisions testify to the Eurosystem’s commitment to aligning its collateral framework with advances in technology, while upholding the principles of adequacy of collateral, safety, efficiency and a level-playing field.
Macroprudential policy and financial stability
Financial Stability Review – November 2026
On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council held an exchange of views on the basis of the November 2026 edition of the Financial Stability Review and authorised its publication on the ECB’s website. In addition to providing an overview of key financial stability vulnerabilities in the euro area, this edition includes three special features. The first discusses the financial stability implications of AI adoption in the real economy and the financial industry. The second explores the complex interplay between AI and cybersecurity. The third assesses the financial stability implications of large initial public offerings and equity issuance in general, as well as how they both interact with the trend towards passive investing. The Financial Stability Review was published on 18 November 2026 on the ECB’s website, together with a related press release.
Banknotes and coins
2026 study on payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area
On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council took note of the results of the 2026 study on the payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area and approved its publication on the ECB’s website. The results show that consumers are increasingly using digital means of payment, while cash continues to play an important role. Moreover, while payment practices are changing, consumers’ own preferences nonetheless remain stable. The results of the study, together with a related press release, are available on the ECB’s website.
Advice on legislation
ECB Opinion on the supervisory independence of the Bank of Greece and prevention of conflicts of interest of its members of staff and governance body
On 4 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/33 at the request of the Greek Ministry of Economy and Finance.
ECB Opinion on designating the Deutsche Bundesbank as a recipient of administrative data for statistical purposes
On 10 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/34 at the request of the Deu

decisions.headline: October US advance goods trade balance -149.5B vs -133.0B expected
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: News] October US advance goods trade balance -149.5B vs -133.0B expected
US goods trade balance numbers
- Prior was -135.9B
That's going leave a dent in GDP forecasts.
For background, the advance international trade in goods report is published by the Census Bureau at 8:30 am ET as part of its Advance Economic Indicators release, roughly four weeks after the reference month ends. It's the earliest monthly read on US trade flows and lands alongside advance estimates for wholesale and retail inventories, making it a key input for GDP tracking.
The headline is the seasonally adjusted US goods trade deficit, the gap between the value of goods imported and exported. Both sides are broken down into six end-use categories: foods, feeds and beverages; industrial supplies and materials; capital goods; automotive vehicles, parts and engines; consumer goods; and other goods. The figures are in nominal dollars on a Census basis.
The advance report covers goods only. Services, where the US runs a surplus in areas such as travel, financial services and intellectual property, are added in the full international trade report from the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis about a week later. That report also revises the advance goods numbers and adds country-level detail.
For markets, the main relevance is GDP. Net exports are a component of growth, so a wider goods deficit generally subtracts from GDP and a narrower one adds to it. Paired with the inventory data released at the same time, the report frequently leads economists and nowcasting models such as the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow to revise their quarterly estimates.
Trade data have been unusually volatile. Surges in imports ahead of tariffs, followed by sharp pullbacks, have caused large swings in the deficit and in quarterly GDP. Big movements in nonmonetary gold, recorded under industrial supplies, have added noise, and economists often exclude gold to judge the underlying trend
Source URL: https://investinglive.com/news/october-us-advance-goods-trade-balance-149-5b-vs-133-0b-expected/

decisions.headline: investingLive European session wrap: Post-Thanksgiving optimism lifts stocks, gold
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: News] investingLive European session wrap: Post-Thanksgiving optimism lifts stocks, gold
Market news from the European morning session - 27 November 2026
Headlines:
- S&P 500 rebounds as growth concerns ease and Nvidia lifts sentiment, but underlying macro headwinds remain unchanged
- Reminder: Wall Street is back today but will dip buyers have the last laugh?
- Gold extends gains after a key technical breakout as broad short-covering improves sentiment
- Gold begins to find its feet again but are buyers out of the woods yet?
- How have interest rate expectations changed after this week's events?
- France Q3 GDP revised lower as economic woes deepen
- France inflation undershoots estimates in November as energy and services price pressures ease
- Spanish inflation comes off the boil in November, offering some respite for the ECB
- Germany unemployment rises more than expected in November as labour market struggles persist
Markets:
- AUD leads, JPY lags on the day
- 10-year Treasury yields up 5 bps to 4.897%
- Gold up 2.9% to $3,668
- Bitcoin up 1.2% to $61,479
- European equities modestly higher; S&P 500 futures +1.6%
It looks like US traders are returning from their Thanksgiving dinner with renewed appetite for risk as well, with US futures rallying ahead of the return of Wall Street later.
Tech shares are leading the charge as investors look to build on Wednesday's turnaround, with S&P 500 futures up by 1.6% and Nasdaq futures up by 2.1% currently. European equities are also joining in on the fun, albeit with considerably more modest gains.
Gold is a standout mover with the precious metal up nearly 3% on the day to $3,668 as the rebound continues. Meanwhile, the dollar is keeping more mixed as it holds its own against the euro and yen but is down against the aussie amid the better risk mood. At the same time though, Treasury yields are nudging up again with 10-year yields up close to 5 bps to near 4.90%.
Typically, higher bond yields make life a little more difficult for both gold and richly valued tech stocks. Yet, both are enjoying quite the rebound today.
That doesn't necessarily mean that something is amiss though. After the beatdown that both have endured this month, some of the buying here could simply be traders unwinding bearish bets rather than investors suddenly turning bullish again. So, there's that to consider.
And that is not to mention that today's trading conditions will offer much clarity either. US markets are back open for an abbreviated session but plenty of traders are likely still enjoying an extended Thanksgiving break. As such, even relatively modest orders can end up moving prices quite considerably amid thinner liquidity conditions.
Then, there's also potential month-end portfolio rebalancing in play and it becomes even harder to separate genuine shifts in market sentiment from money being moved around for largely mechanical reasons.
But for now though, we're definitely seeing dip buyers and the optimists find themselves some much needed breathing room. At this juncture, there's certainly the temptation to buy the dip. However, let's be reminded that there's a difference between markets finding a bit of relief and traders finding their conviction again.
There are definitely signs of the latter, more so than earlier in the week, but the blurry trading conditions today will make it hard to tell for sure if we're truly back with a bang. I reckon we'll only get a better sense of that come next week.
Source URL: https://investinglive.com/news/investinglive-european-session-wrap-post-thanksgiving-optimism-lifts-stocks-gold/

Interest rate expectations remained largely unchanged this week given the lack of major macro or geopolitical developments. The prolonged US-Iran stalemate, growth concerns and persistent inflation risks continue to shape the outlook. The more notable moves came from Canada and Australia, where central bank commentary and economic data led to some changes in interest rate expectations.
The Bank of Canada saw the most notable hawkish repricing. Hawkish remarks from BoC members this week reinforced expectations of another rate hike coming in December and potentially more in 2027. I think the BoC is making a policy mistake given subdued inflationary pressures, soft labour market and negative growth drivers.
On the RBA side, we've got some more dovish repricing despite hotter-than-expected inflation data this week. The market is looking beyond the near-term conditions and placing greater weight on weakening economic activity confirmed by the softer PMIs on Monday and the deteriorating labour market conditions.

decisions.headline: Germany unemployment rises more than expected in November as labour market struggles persist
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: News] Germany unemployment rises more than expected in November as labour market struggles persist
Germany's labour market continues to struggle as unemployment rises in November
- Germany November unemployment change 9k vs 4k expected
- Prior 4k
- Germany November unemployment rate 6.4% vs 6.4% expected
- Prior 6.4%
The number of people out of work in Germany rose by more than expected in November, though the jobless rate is seen holding steady on the month at 6.4%. Overall, the total number of unemployed persons rose to 3.025 million in seasonally adjusted terms.
But when looking at the unadjusted total, it fell by 19,000 to 2.936 million in November with the labour office noting that the decline reflected the end of the autumn seasonal pickup. However, I'd put more weight on the seasonally adjusted figures here as they strip out the usual seasonal fluctuations and offer a better indication of the underlying health of the labour market.
As for the overall report, the labour office noted that "the trend of recent months is continuing" and that "the slight economic recovery has not led to revival in the labour market in November".
If you couple that with the subdued consumer confidence figures yesterday, then you can see why there are still concerns about the sustainability of the recovery. If households become more worried about job security, they're more likely to hold back on spending. That will then give businesses even less incentive to expand and hire.
In turn, it also makes life more complicated for the ECB, which is still having to contend with elevated inflation despite pockets of economic weakness across the region.
Looking to next year, I'd keep a close eye on whether the weakness in hiring starts to translate into more widespread job cuts. A more sluggish labour market is one thing but a more pronounced deterioration in employment could make Germany's economic recovery considerably harder to sustain.

decisions.raw_text:
[ECB] ECB Consumer Expectations Survey results – October 2026
- PRESS RELEASE
ECB Consumer Expectations Survey results – October 2026
27 November 2026
Compared with September 2026:
- median consumer perceptions of inflation over the past 12 months and expectations for inflation over the next 12 months increased significantly, while median expectations for inflation three years ahead increased slightly and those for five years ahead were unchanged;
- expectations for nominal income growth over the next 12 months declined, while expectations for spending growth over the next 12 months were unchanged;
- expectations for economic growth over the next 12 months increased, while the expected unemployment rate in 12 months’ time decreased;
- expectations for growth in the price of homes over the next 12 months decreased, while expectations for mortgage interest rates in 12 months’ time remained unchanged.
Inflation
In October the median rate of perceived inflation over the previous 12 months increased to 4.1% from 3.6% in September and stood at its highest level since July 2024. Median expectations for inflation over the next 12 months also rose to 3.5% from 3.1%, but remained below the level reached at the start of the conflict in March 2026 (4.0%). Median expectations for inflation three years ahead increased to 3.0% from 2.9%, returning to the March 2026 level. Median expectations for inflation five years ahead were unchanged at 2.5% for the third consecutive month, the highest level since the start of the series in August 2022. Uncertainty about expectations for inflation over the next 12 months increased for the second consecutive month, remaining higher than the level prior to the start of the conflict in the Middle East. Respondents in the bottom income quintile continued to report higher inflation perceptions and expectations, on average, than those in the top quintile. Younger respondents (aged 18-34) continued to report lower inflation perceptions and expectations than older respondents (aged 35-54 and 55-70).
Inflation results
Income and consumption
Consumers’ expectations for nominal income growth over the next 12 months fell to 0.6% from 1.1% in September. While expectations declined across all income quintiles, the decline was most pronounced in the bottom income quintile (by 0.7 percentage points to 0.8%) and in the top quintile (by 0.8 percentage points to 0.4%). Perceived nominal spending growth over the previous 12 months increased to 5.4% from 5.3% in September, while expected nominal spending growth over the next 12 months was unchanged at 3.7%.
Income and consumption results
Economic growth and labour market
Expectations for economic growth over the next 12 months increased in October to -1.3% from -1.5% in September. Expectations for the unemployment rate 12 months ahead decreased to 11.0% from 11.3% in September. As observed in previous months, households in the bottom income quintile expected the highest unemployment rate 12 months ahead (13.3%), while households in the top income quintile expected the lowest rate (9.5%). Consumers continued to expect the future unemployment rate to be only slightly higher than the perceived current unemployment rate (10.4%), suggesting a broadly stable labour market outlook. Quarterly data revealed a somewhat mixed labour market sentiment. Unemployed respondents reported a lower expected probability of finding a job over the next three months, at 29.6% in October compared with 30.8% in July. Employed respondents reported a lower expected probability of job loss over the next three months, at 9.4% in October compared with 9.8% in July.

decisions.headline: European stock market open: The rebound party rolls on
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Stocks] European stock market open: The rebound party rolls on
European stocks extend gains as US futures point to a strong return for Wall Street
- Eurostoxx +1.1%
- Germany DAX +0.7%
- France CAC 40 +0.4%
- UK FTSE +0.7%
- Spain IBEX +0.9%
- Italy FTSE MIB +1.5%
It looks like dip buyers are hoping to squeeze in a little bit of joy out of what has otherwise been a rather miserable month for equities.
European stocks are building on yesterday's impressive gains, while S&P 500 futures are now up 1.8% and Nasdaq futures up 2.5%. Tech shares are once again leading the charge, which is encouraging considering that they have been at the heart of much of the market's troubles this month.
European investors already had a chance to celebrate Wednesday's turnaround on Wall Street during the Thanksgiving holiday yesterday. So, today's gains are more about extending that optimism as US traders return to their desks later in the day.
My only reservation is that we're heading into what will be an abbreviated trading session in the US, with the Thanksgiving holiday still somewhat hanging over. That means we will see thinner liquidity conditions and potential month-end flows also in play.
As such, lesser market participants will mean less money to move markets and so the size of any rally today might not necessarily reflect the strength of conviction behind it.
If anything else, I reckon the main focus will be on whether tech shares can hold on to their gains after the opening bell and whether the buying extends to other corners of the market. At this stage, a broader recovery would be far more encouraging than another tech-led bounce alone.
For now at least, dip buyers have the upper hand at the European market open. However, next week should offer a much better test of whether this recovery has legs. That is once liquidity conditions normalise and we put any shenanigans from November's portfolio rebalancing behind us.

decisions.headline: Spanish inflation comes off the boil in November, offering some respite for the ECB
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: News] Spanish inflation comes off the boil in November, offering some respite for the ECB
Spanish inflation takes a welcome step lower but the ECB still faces a difficult balancing act going into next year
- Spain November preliminary CPI +4.1% vs +4.6% y/y expected
- Prior +4.9%
- Spain November preliminary HICP +4.1% vs +4.7% y/y expected
- Prior +4.9%
Much like the French report earlier, Spain's inflation numbers are also seen cooling off in November. After nearly hitting 5% in October, headline annual inflation is seen dropping back to 4.1% this month. The added good news is that core annual inflation was also estimated to drop to 2.6% in November, as compared to the 3.1% reading in the month before.
That being said, these figures are all still too high for any comfort for the ECB. And that's the troubling part for the central bank as they are dealing with quite an array of inflation backdrops across the region at this stage.
But as a whole, policymakers are arguably very much concerned about the risks of potential second-round effects. So, that remains the priority in terms of policy setting.
As things stand, they are likely to be able to get away with another rate hike in December. And the market pricing reflects roughly 93% odds of a 25 bps move already. But in looking to next year, the challenge will be how the central bank balances any further tightening measures against slowing economic growth.
The fiscal risks from France and now more trouble from US tariffs will make things even more challenging for the ECB. So, therein lies their predicament as we move to the final stages of the year.
Source URL: https://investinglive.com/news/spanish-inflation-comes-off-the-boil-in-november-offering-some-respite-for-the-ecb/

decisions.headline: France Q3 GDP revised lower as economic woes deepen
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: News] France Q3 GDP revised lower as economic woes deepen
France's economy contracts more than initially estimated, complicating the ECB's policy outlook heading into next year
- France Q3 final GDP -0.2% vs -0.1% q/q prelim
- Prior 0.0%
Ouch. France was already the troubling spot in the euro area and the negative revision to the preliminary GDP estimates only continues to underscore that notion. In volume terms, the French economy contracted by 0.2% in Q3 following some tentative stability in the previous quarter.
Domestic demand was pretty much subdued, stagnating on the quarter, while inventory changes contributed to 0.3% to quarterly GDP with net foreign trade being the main drag with a negative contribution of 0.6% on the quarter.
Overall, the French economy is seen growing by just 0.1% so far this year and that is hardly encouraging for Europe's second-largest economy.
As such, this won't steer the conversation away from stagflationary risks as we head into next year. The only good news is that the latest French inflation numbers for November is at least showing some signs of cooling, affording the ECB some added breathing room in looking to the French economy as a whole.
Source URL: https://investinglive.com/news/france-q3-gdp-revised-lower-as-economic-woes-deepen/

decisions.headline: France inflation undershoots estimates in November as energy and services price pressures ease
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: News] France inflation undershoots estimates in November as energy and services price pressures ease
French inflation cools more than expected in November, offering the ECB some breathing room amid stagflation risks
- France November preliminary CPI +2.9% vs +3.2% y/y expected
- Prior +3.4%
- France November preliminary HICP +3.2% vs +3.6% y/y expected
- Prior +3.7%
Well, that's some good news for the French economy as inflation pressures are seen cooling back a little in November. The drop here is even below analyst estimates, with headline annual inflation dropping back below 3%. The monthly reading also shows that French inflation should ease by 0.7% in November, after having risen by 0.4% in October.
Looking at the details, energy inflation falling off is a key factor driving that development. Of note, energy prices are seen rising by 19.2% in November compared to the 24.1% increase in October.
That being said, core prices are also likely to come off the boil as services inflation cooled as well. Services prices were seen down to 2.3% in November compared to 2.6% in the month before.
All in all, the ECB can take some comfort in that as this will reduce stagflationary risks in Europe's second-largest economy. But even then, price pressures are admittedly still on the higher side and policymakers cannot rest on their laurels just yet.
For now, all of this still supports the argument that they may perhaps get away with another rate hike. But after, they will have to seriously consider the balance of risks between overtightening monetary policy and the necessity to tame the inflation monster amid potential second-round effects.
In other words, they will still be in a tough spot in trying to decide on policy so as to risk sending the economy off the ledge or allowing inflation pressures to grow to be too overwhelming. That will be the key challenge for policymakers next year.

decisions.headline: Warsh's 2018 dilemma returns as an AI stock rout meets a Fed bent on taming inflation
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] Warsh's 2018 dilemma returns as an AI stock rout meets a Fed bent on taming inflation
The AI stock rout is testing Fed Chair Warsh, who urged a pause in the 2018 selloff. With core PCE at 3.3%, officials seem untroubled by falling stocks and markets expect a December 8-9 hike, though a disorderly rout could change the calculus.
The key idea
- The Federal Reserve is currently prioritizing fighting inflation, even if it means tolerating a stock market decline.
- This is different from 2018, when the Fed was more sensitive to falling stock prices because inflation was already at its target.
- The "Fed put" is the market's belief that the central bank will step in to prevent significant stock market drops. The Fed is trying to avoid reinforcing this idea now.
Reader questions
- Why is the Fed more willing to let stocks fall now compared to 2018? The main reason is inflation; it is much higher now than in 2018, so the Fed is focused on bringing prices down.
- What does "tightening" mean in this context? Tightening refers to actions by the Fed, like raising interest rates, that aim to slow down the economy and reduce inflation.
- Why are credit markets important for the Fed's decision making? Stress in credit markets, especially for heavily indebted companies, could signal broader economic problems and might make the Fed reconsider its stance more than just falling stock prices.
The message for equity investors is that the bar for Fed support is much higher than in 2018. With core inflation at 3.3%, an orderly decline in AI-linked stocks is more likely to be treated as useful tightening than as a reason to pause. That keeps a December hike firmly priced and supports the dollar and short-dated Treasury yields. The key signal is the Fed's December projections, which are expected to show more hikes ahead. Credit markets are the trigger to watch: stress among heavily indebted AI-related borrowers would be far more likely to shift the Fed's stance than falling share prices alone. For gold, which pays no yield, a Fed still focused on hiking remains a headwind.
---
Kevin Warsh once urged the Fed to back off as stocks slid in 2018, but with inflation stuck well above target and AI demand running hot, his Fed looks far more willing to let a market rout do some of its work.
Summary:
- The AI-driven stock selloff could force Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh to choose between hiking rates and letting markets tighten conditions for him
- Warsh urged the Fed to pause during the December 2018 selloff, when inflation was only just at target
- Core PCE inflation rose to 3.3% in October from 3.1%, and has been above target for more than five years
- Fed officials increasingly see AI-driven demand as a source of persistent price pressure
- Markets expect a hike at the December 8-9 meeting, with officials divided on how far to go after that
- A disorderly selloff, especially in credit tied to more than $800 billion of AI-related debt, remains the bigger concern
The rout in AI-linked stocks is testing how much market turmoil the Federal Reserve is willing to tolerate in its fight against inflation, and so far the answer appears to be a lot. If the selloff deepens, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh may have to choose between delivering on his tough talk on prices and relying on falling markets to do some of the tightening for him.
As Nick Timiraos reported in The Wall Street Journal (gated), Warsh has faced this dilemma before, from the outside. In December 2018, with stocks about 11% below their peak, he co-wrote a piece urging the Fed to pause its tightening. The Fed hiked anyway, the selloff accelerated into the worst December for stocks since 1931, and officials quickly signalled they were in no rush to move again.
The parallels with today are striking. Then, as now, a first-year Fed chair was raising rates into falling stocks and a stronger dollar, during a geopolitical shock and after a midterm setback for President Trump

Profits at China's industrial firms rose 20.1% y/y in October from 14.4% in September, lifting year-to-date growth to 16%. Electronics makers led while furniture slumped, and weak domestic demand leaves firms reliant on exports as tariff risks rise.
The key idea

- How do these profit figures influence currency markets? Stronger industrial profits can sometimes support currencies like the yuan, but the article suggests other factors like trade headlines might have a bigger impact.
The data offers some support for Chinese and wider Asian technology supply-chain stocks, where profits are clearly strongest. Its value as a signal for the broader economy is limited, though, because consumer-facing sectors are still struggling. For commodities, stronger factory earnings are mildly supportive for industrial metals, but persistent property weakness caps the upside for steel-linked inputs such as iron ore. Any new US or EU trade restrictions would hit the export-dependent firms that drove October's gains.

The key idea
- Gold is currently trading more like a "risk asset" than a traditional safe haven; its price movements are closely linked to stock market performance.
- When investors sell stocks to cover losses, they also sell assets like gold to raise cash, which pushes gold prices down.
Reader questions
- What does it mean for gold to trade as a "risk asset" rather than a "haven"? When gold acts as a risk asset, its price tends to fall when the stock market falls, similar to how other riskier investments behave. A haven asset, by contrast, usually holds its value or even rises during times of market uncertainty.
- Why is the $3,400 level important for gold? This price point is considered a major support level; if gold falls below it, it could signal a significant downward trend and undo a previous milestone in its bull market.
- How do tariffs affect precious metals like silver and platinum? While tariffs can sometimes be positive for gold, new tariffs could hurt industries that use a lot of silver and platinum, potentially lowering demand and prices for those metals.
Gold is trading as a risk asset rather than a haven, so equity markets have become the key driver. Another leg lower in stocks would raise the chance of a test of $3,400, while a stabilisation would ease the forced selling. Silver and platinum group metals face an extra layer of risk from tariffs that could hit the industries using them, even though HSBC still expects silver to be in deficit. US tariff announcements are worth watching, especially any aimed at Mexico or Canada, which HSBC sees as the exception that could lift silver. decisions.headline: OCBC sees the Indian rupee strengthening to 92.10 per dollar by end-2027 as oil relief builds
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Forex] OCBC sees the Indian rupee strengthening to 92.10 per dollar by end-2027 as oil relief builds
OCBC forecasts USD/INR at 92.10 by end-2027 as lower oil, recovering equity inflows and possible global bond index inclusion support the rupee. RBI reserve rebuilding should slow gains, and oil remains the near-term risk with Brent seen at $100.
The key idea
- The Indian rupee's value is significantly influenced by global oil prices and foreign investment flows.
- When oil prices are lower, India's import costs decrease, which generally strengthens the rupee.
- Foreign exchange reserves are the foreign currencies held by a country's central bank; rebuilding these reserves can slow down a currency's appreciation.
Reader questions
- Why is oil such a "swing factor" for the Indian rupee? India imports most of its crude oil; therefore, higher oil prices mean India needs to spend more foreign currency to buy oil, which weakens the rupee.
- What does "one-way bets against the currency" mean? This refers to traders consistently betting that the rupee will weaken; the RBI's measures make it more expensive for them to do so, reducing sharp currency swings.
- How does inclusion in a global bond index help the rupee? If India's bonds are included in a major index, more foreign investors will buy them, bringing in foreign currency and increasing demand for the rupee.
For the rupee, oil is the swing factor. With OCBC keeping its end-2026 Brent forecast at $100 a barrel, any fresh attack on Gulf energy infrastructure or disruption around Hormuz could quickly reverse recent gains, since India imports most of its crude. The RBI's measures make one-way bets against the currency more expensive, which should limit sharp swings in USD/INR in either direction. A firm decision on India's inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Index would be the clearest upside catalyst, as it would bring passive bond inflows. RBI reserve rebuilding means rupee strength is likely to be gradual, which suits carry trades more than outright momentum bets.
After a punishing year of oil shocks and outflows, the rupee has found its footing on RBI measures, cheaper crude and returning equity money, and OCBC expects gradual gains into 2027 as the central bank rebuilds its reserves.

decisions.headline: Goldman says hyperscalers can easily earn 15% on AI, but neoclouds face a utilisation trap
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Stocks] Goldman says hyperscalers can easily earn 15% on AI, but neoclouds face a utilisation trap
Goldman's Eric Sheridan says the six largest US hyperscalers can easily earn 15%-plus returns on AI spending, but investor Chamath Palihapitiya warns neoclouds depend on big companies finally seeing a payoff, which has yet to happen at scale.
The key idea
- The article discusses how different types of companies are positioned to profit from the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. It highlights a potential divide between large tech companies and smaller, specialized firms.
- "Hyperscalers" are the very large cloud computing providers, like Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure, that have massive infrastructure and diverse revenue streams. They are seen as more resilient in the AI investment cycle.
- "Neoclouds" are newer, specialized companies that primarily rent out GPU capacity for AI computations. They face higher risks if demand for AI computing power does not meet their fixed costs.
Reader questions
- Why is "return on invested capital" important here? This metric shows how efficiently a company is using its capital to generate profits. For AI investments, it indicates whether the money spent on AI infrastructure is actually leading to profitable growth.
- What is the "utilization trap" for neoclouds? This refers to the risk that neocloud companies might build out significant computing capacity but then struggle to find enough customers to use it. If their capacity is not highly utilized, they may not cover their substantial fixed costs for chips and data centers.
- Why do big companies not yet seeing returns from AI affect neoclouds more? If large corporations are not yet seeing clear profits from their AI projects, their demand for computing power from neoclouds might slow down. This directly impacts neoclouds, which rely heavily on this demand to fill their capacity and generate revenue.
The views point to a widening gap in how investors treat the AI trade. Hyperscaler stocks and investment-grade bonds look the most defensible, given their strong balance sheets and cash flows outside AI. Neocloud equity and high-yield credit carry the most risk if utilisation disappoints. Goldman's credit team expects the high-yield market for AI deals to split more sharply, with investors favouring top-tier developers and projects backed by solid contracts. Chipmakers and memory suppliers ultimately depend on the same thing as the neoclouds: evidence that companies using AI are earning a return. The next earnings round's commentary on returns on capital is likely to move the whole complex.
--
Goldman's analysis suggests the tech giants can comfortably earn a return on their AI build-out, but the neoclouds renting out GPU capacity are exposed if corporate customers keep failing to turn AI spending into profit.
Summary:
- Goldman's Eric Sheridan estimates the six largest US hyperscalers can easily earn a return on invested capital of 15% or more on AI spending
- Hyperscaler revenue backlogs have grown sharply, and only part of them needs to convert to revenue to reach that return
- Social Capital's Chamath Palihapitiya warns that neoclouds have short-term revenue but long-dated, fixed obligations
- Big companies are not yet seeing returns from AI that show up in earnings, which caps demand for computing power
- Hyperscalers need around $1.4 trillion in cumulative revenue over 2028 to 2030 to earn 15% on their 2026 and 2027 investment
- Weaker demand, tighter access to capital or a shortage of power could stall the investment cycle
Is the artificial intelligence spending boom built to last? Goldman Sachs put that question to two people who see the cycle from very different vantage points, and their answers point the same way. The biggest technology companies are well placed to ride out a slowdown. The risk is concentrated among newer, more heavily indebted players further down the chain.

[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Commodities] Gold's 37% slide from record looks overdone, says Saxo's Hansen, but $3,590 is the test
Gold has swung from 45% above its 200-day average in January to about 20% below, and Saxo's Ole Hansen sees signs of selling exhaustion. A daily close above about $3,590 would confirm a rebound toward $3,700; a break below Wednesday's low voids it.
The key idea
- Gold prices are currently more influenced by the U.S. dollar's strength and expectations for U.S. interest rates than by its traditional role as a safe haven.
- "Short covering" refers to buying back borrowed shares or contracts to close out a short position; this buying can cause a rapid price increase.
Reader questions
- Why does a strong U.S. dollar impact gold prices? A stronger dollar makes gold, which is priced in dollars, more expensive for buyers using other currencies, often leading to decreased demand and lower prices.
- What are "real yields" and why do they matter for gold? Real yields are the return an investor gets after accounting for inflation; higher real yields make interest-bearing assets more attractive than non-yielding gold.
- Why is the 200-day moving average mentioned as a key technical level? The 200-day moving average is a widely watched indicator that helps traders identify long-term trends; prices significantly above or below it can signal overbought or oversold conditions.
Gold's moves are being set by the dollar and US rate pricing, not by safe-haven demand, so US data and Fed commentary will matter more than geopolitical headlines for any rebound. Because speculative positioning has been cut so hard, short covering could make any bounce sharp, especially in silver, the most stretched metal. A failure back below Wednesday's low would suggest forced selling has further to run. That would be a risk for miners and leveraged exposure. A softer dollar or a dovish shift in Fed expectations is the catalyst most likely to turn a technical rebound into a lasting one.

decisions.headline: ECB picks Spain's Hernández de Cos as president, with 3 tests waiting from day one
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] ECB picks Spain's Hernández de Cos as president, with 3 tests waiting from day one
EU leaders picked Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde as ECB president in February. The BIS chief faces an immediate test from France's volatile bond market, with a presidential vote due two months after he takes office.
The key idea
- The appointment of a new European Central Bank (ECB) president can significantly influence bond markets, especially for countries with high debt.
- Quantitative easing (QE) is a monetary policy where a central bank buys government bonds or other financial assets to inject money into the economy and lower interest rates.
Reader questions
- Why does the new ECB president's stance on quantitative easing and fiscal discipline matter for French bonds? The market will be watching to see if the new president is more likely to use tools like QE to support French debt, especially given the country's upcoming election and volatile bond market.
- What are "French spreads" and why are they tied to the election campaign? French spreads refer to the difference in yield between French government bonds and a benchmark, typically German bonds; this spread reflects the perceived risk of French debt, and an uncertain election can increase that risk.
For bonds, the appointment matters most for the gap between French and German yields. Markets may treat a president who backed quantitative easing as a slightly firmer safety net for French debt, but his record on fiscal discipline makes a blanket rescue unlikely. That leaves French spreads tied to the election campaign more than to the ECB. The euro's immediate reaction is likely to be muted, since Hernández de Cos is seen as a continuity candidate, not someone who will change the direction of rates. Brunnermeier as chief economist is worth watching, as his academic work on financial stability could shape how the bank thinks about stepping into markets.

New Zealand consumer confidence rose 4 points to 100.2 in November, the highest since January but below the 112 average. Two-year inflation expectations fell to 3.9% from 4.2%, the lowest since January 2025, as fuel prices at the pump dropped.
The key idea
- Consumer confidence surveys offer a snapshot of how households feel about their financial situation and the economy.
- When confidence rises, it often suggests people might be more willing to spend, which can boost economic activity.
- Inflation expectations, which are what people believe future price increases will be, are a key part of these surveys.
Reader questions
- Why does falling inflation expectations matter for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand?
Falling inflation expectations can reduce pressure on the central bank to raise interest rates, as it suggests price pressures might be easing. This gives them more flexibility in their monetary policy decisions.
- What does "hawkish shift in the policy outlook" mean?
A hawkish shift means the central bank is becoming more inclined to raise interest rates or tighten monetary policy to control inflation. The article suggests falling inflation expectations might make the central bank less likely to adopt such a stance.
- How does consumer confidence relate to the New Zealand dollar?
Generally, stronger consumer confidence and a healthier economic outlook can support a country's currency. However, if falling inflation expectations lead to less aggressive interest rate hikes, it could slightly weaken the currency, as suggested in the article.
Households' inflation expectations have fallen sharply from their April peak, which eases one worry for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. That leans slightly against any hawkish shift in the policy outlook and is a mild negative for the New Zealand dollar at the margin. The survey's market impact is usually small, though, and moves in global risk appetite and the US dollar are likely to matter more for the currency. The main sensitivity to watch is oil: these readings now follow pump prices closely, so a renewed jump in crude would probably undo much of this month's improvement.

[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] EU leaders set to confirm backing for Spain's De Cos as next ECB President - report
Reuters report cites EU diplomats
Reuters reports, citing EU diplomats, that EU leaders are set to sign off on Pablo Hernández de Cos as the next president of the European Central Bank.
This has been well telegraphed. Christine Lagarde is leaving early. She steps down on February 7, nine months before her eight-year term was due to end in October 2027. The timing is political. Leaving early lets EU leaders lock in a successor before April's French presidential election, where polls favour Marine Le Pen (and will be a major event in FX markets next year).
The race was really decided when Paris and Berlin agreed on a deal. France backed De Cos for the top job and proposed a Frenchwoman for the market operations role. That left Germany free to nominate the chief economist, and Berlin wants that seat for Princeton professor Markus Brunnermeier. The deal squeezed out Klaas Knot. Dutch media reported last week that he's expected to withdraw. The formal sign-off is aimed at the December 17-18 summit.
In terms of policy, De Cos was seen as slightly more dovish than Knot. More important is the backstop angle. He's a southern European and a Draghi ally, which reinforces the view that Frankfurt will step in if spreads blow out, whether that's true or not. T
There's nothing here for EUR/USD today. It's priced, and the ECB is a committee. Still, at the margin it's a mild dovish tilt and a vote for tighter BTP and OAT spreads into 2027. The next thing to watch is who gets the chief economist job. With Brunnermeier as the German pick, the hawks would keep a strong voice on the Executive Board and we're back to the typical dovish tilt at the ECB with the hawkish criticism coming from the Germans.
Today, the euro is up 14 pips to 1.0985.

EUR/USD could find further upside support if weaker US data or less hawkish Fed commentary triggers a dovish repricing in interest rate expectations. The dollar has been supported by safe-haven flows and the hawkish repricing, while the euro still faces headwinds from France’s unresolved budget issues and uneven growth. However, with the US dollar heavily overbought and EUR/USD largely driven by USD dynamics, a shift in Fed expectations could outweigh euro-related concerns.
USD:
The US dollar has found support recently from a
hawkish repricing in interest rate expectations following Governor Waller’s
remarks, in which he even floated the possibility of a larger 50 bps hike at
the December meeting. Higher-than-expected US inflation data added to the
hawkish sentiment.
Moreover, the greenback benefited from safe-haven
flows as global growth concerns intensified amid a more hawkish Fed, the
prolonged US-Iran stalemate and a global stock market selloff.
Those same growth concerns, though, triggered a dovish
repricing of Fed rate hike expectations further out the curve, as markets
anticipated that the stock market rout could significantly weigh on the broader
economy. This has caused the yield differential to favour the upside for the
EUR/USD pair, although the greenback remained resilient thanks to safe-haven
demand.
Looking ahead, we might see the US dollar coming under
more pressure in case the Fed sounds less hawkish than expected or the economic
data triggers a dovish repricing in interest rates expectations.
EUR:
On the EUR side, the ECB is
widely expected to raise interest rates by 25 bps at the December meeting and deliver
one final hike in June 2027. Growth is holding up well, but the recovery
remains uneven, with France being a drag. Inflation and energy-related risks
are still complicating the ECB’s job of getting inflation sustainably back to
target.
France's 2027 budget battle
is still ongoing, and the government is struggling to get its deficit-reduction
plans through parliament. So, the French fiscal story remains unresolved. The
key risk for French bonds is that parliament waters down the government's
consolidation measures, leaving France with a higher deficit for longer. This
could keep the French-German 10-year yield spread and the euro under pressure.
At the end of the day, the EUR/USD
pair is 80% driven by what happens with the US dollar, so a dovish repricing in
Fed interest rate expectations will likely outweigh euro-related woes,
especially given the overbought US dollar positioning.

ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME
On the daily chart, we can
see that EURUSD is consolidating near recent
lows as traders await new catalysts. If we get a pullback into the downward
trendline, we can expect the sellers to lean on it, with a defined risk above

1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

There wasn't all too much in European trading today, with market players bracing themselves for a bit of a break in the second half of the week.
The Thanksgiving holiday is upon us and that will see US markets closed today before only opening for more of an abbreviated session tomorrow. As such, thinner liquidity conditions will be a key consideration and that means any modest order flows or sudden headlines could lead to exacerbated price movements in the days ahead.
But so far today, we are seeing a calmer mood in broader markets with European stocks catching a strong bounce after the Wall Street turnaround yesterday. Regional indices are holding gains well over 1% in erasing the more negative mood over the past few sessions, and even looking to post a weekly gain now. The DAX is up by 1.8% on the day with the CAC 40 up by 1.6% currently.
In the absence of US markets, the dollar is keeping calmer while showing little interest as the recent rally hits the pause button for a moment. EUR/USD is flat at 1.0974 with USD/JPY up by just 0.1% to 159.25 on the day.
As for the commodities space, we are seeing oil catch a little bounce with WTI crude up 1% to $84.51 while gold is struggling to build on yesterday's bounce and hold above $3,500 as the precious metal is down 0.3% to $3,571 today.
With the Thanksgiving holiday kicking into gear now, I'd be particularly wary of reading too much into any technical breakouts or breakdowns during the coming two days.
As much as the turnaround yesterday was quite encouraging, the real test for dip buyers will be whether they can continue to build on that momentum once the usual crowd returns next week. In the meantime, we'll have to deal with a quieter period with potential for some volatility bouts amid thinner liquidity conditions and also month-end flows perhaps.
For those enjoying the holidays, have a good break and I wish you a pleasant turkey day!

[ECB] Meeting of 28-29 October 2026
Meeting of 28-29 October 2026
Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday, 28-29 October 2026
26 November 2026
1. Review of financial, economic and monetary developments and policy options
Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel started her presentation on the latest financial market developments with the observation that higher energy prices since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 9-10 September 2026 had reinforced concerns about persistent inflationary pressures. At the same time, market attention had shifted towards fiscal dynamics and concerns about the increasingly debt-financed artificial intelligence (AI) investment cycle.
Energy price pressures had intensified substantially since the September meeting, pushing oil and gas prices above the adverse scenario of the September 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area. In response to renewed tensions in the Middle East, the latest oil futures curve had shifted markedly higher compared with the baseline of the September projections and had also moved visibly above the adverse scenario over the short term. The repricing in gas markets had been even more pronounced, with the futures curve currently standing well above the adverse scenario over the entire horizon.
Diesel refining margins stood at a historically high level, with euro area diesel crack spreads – the differences between wholesale prices and crude oil prices – above the levels observed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Freight rates from the Gulf region to Europe had surged to record highs, while the probability of a US-Iran peace deal by the end of 2026 was at its lowest since the start of the war in the Middle East. The increase in energy prices was reflected in inflation compensation. Inflation fixings throughout 2026 and 2027 had shifted higher, peaking at 4.5% for January 2027 and remaining above 2.5% until the first quarter of 2028, while inflation fixings for 2028 were broadly unchanged. Option-implied inflation risks continued to be skewed to the upside over the next two years and five years.
Despite the sharp increase in energy prices and the deterioration in the inflation outlook, expectations for the key ECB interest rates stood near their September levels. The one-year overnight index swap (OIS) rate one year ahead had decoupled from energy prices, consistent with communication that interest rates would not move in lockstep with energy costs. Immediately after the Governing Council’s September monetary policy meeting, the OIS forward curve had shifted markedly higher, temporarily pricing in more than four additional 25 basis point hikes over the next 12 months, before investors pared back expectations to just under three additional hikes. Market pricing adjusted for term premia pointed to an expected peak in the deposit facility rate at around 3%, implying a more pronounced tightening than the median expectation of participants in the Survey of Monetary Analysts, which foresaw only one more hike.
Euro area risk-free rates had stabilised and, at longer tenors, had even declined since the September meeting, while US rates had risen across maturities on the back of higher real rates. The divergence between real yields in the euro area and the United States was consistent with investors’ perceptions of a more dynamic US economy.
The rise in euro area ten-year rates relative to the average in 2024 had been driven primarily by higher real term premia, reflecting increased uncertainty about the long-run macroeconomic outlook and a growing net supply of public and private debt. [ECB] Climate change indicators: November 2026
- PRESS RELEASE
Climate change indicators: November 2026
26 November 2026
- Carbon emissions financed by euro area banks and investment funds declined between 2018 and 2025
- Physical risk indicators highlight rising heat and wildfire risks under future climate scenarios
- Latest release further improves quality and coverage of climate risk indicators
The European Central Bank (ECB) has published updated statistical climate indicators to assess developments in transition and physical risks related to climate change. These updates incorporate enhanced methodologies, new data sources and more detailed information, enabling more precise tracking of decarbonisation efforts and the impact of climate-related hazards. The sustainable finance indicators, which form part of the statistical climate change indicators, are scheduled to be updated by January 2027.
Transition risk indicators
The latest release of carbon emissions and transition risk indicators confirms a continuation of the downward trend in climate-related exposures and risks in the portfolios of euro area financial institutions. In particular, the latest results point to an ongoing reduction of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions embedded in banks’ portfolios, without a reduction in their lending volumes to the emitting non-financial companies.
For banks’ loan portfolios (Chart 1, panel a), the latest calculations and estimates show that financed direct emissions (Scope 1) decreased by more than one-third between 2018 and 2025. They fell by 36%, from 221 to 142 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent.[1] Thanks to methodological enhancements, the carbon emissions indicators now additionally cover indirect emissions (Scopes 2 and 3) embedded in banks’ loan portfolios. These emissions followed a similar downward trend: emissions associated with energy consumption (Scope 2) declined by 56%, while those linked to other production inputs consumed (upstream Scope 3) declined by 32% over the same period.
Similarly, for the securities portfolios of non-money market investment funds (Chart 1, panel b), the latest calculations and estimates show that financed direct emissions decreased by 34% between 2018 and 2025, from 499 to 328 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent. Indirect emissions (Scope 2) declined by 44%, from 121 to 69 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent.
These reductions in financed emissions occurred despite increases in the value of the portfolios of in-scope instruments: 17% for bank loans and 95% for investment funds’ securities portfolios. These increases were mainly driven by price effects.
A downward trend is also evident in the carbon intensity of creditors’ portfolios, measured as emissions per unit of revenue using the weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) indicator. This provides a further indication of the decarbonisation of euro area financial portfolios.

Gold remains caught between forced liquidations during equity selloffs and upside pressure from a hawkish Fed repricing when sentiment improves. because the US dollar and real yields get support from the hawkish repricing.

gold will likely need support from a dovish repricing in interest rate

decisions.headline: European stock market open: Stocks surge after stunning Wall Street turnaround
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Stocks] European stock market open: Stocks surge after stunning Wall Street turnaround
European equities rally strongly as investors take comfort in Wall Street's comeback ahead of the Thanksgiving break
- Eurostoxx +1.8%
- Germany DAX +1.6%
- France CAC 40 +1.6%
- UK FTSE +1.3%
- Spain IBEX +1.6%
- Italy FTSE MIB +2.1%
What a difference a day can make in markets. This time yesterday, risk sentiment was in the dumps as US futures were losing altitude quickly and that even threatened a poor day for European stocks. Fast forward to today, we're now seeing equities enjoy quite the relief rally after Wall Street pulled off a rather remarkable comeback in trading yesterday.
The S&P 500 finished lower by just 0.3% after having been down by more than 3% at one point. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq salvaged a 0.6% decline after having been down by more than 4%. The Dow even managed to sneak into positive territory, ending the day higher by 0.3%.
Considering how ugly things were looking midway through European trading yesterday, it's no surprise to see regional equities playing catch-up in a big way today.
All that being said though, do be reminded that there is a bit of an awkward pause to the dip buying momentum as a whole. The Thanksgiving holiday is upon us and US stock markets are closed today with only an abbreviated session set for tomorrow. In other words, European stocks will be left to fend for themselves over the next two days without much direction from Wall Street.
As such, I would be careful about reading too much into the gains today - especially with thinner liquidity conditions potentially exaggerating market moves in either direction. The rebound yesterday was encouraging and optimistic, but it doesn't undo weeks of technical damage yet.

German consumer sentiment edged up heading into December but continues to remain subdued as a whole, according to the latest GfK/NIM survey.

[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Commodities] Ray Dalio's 10-15% gold call resurfaces as bullion tries to find its feet
Ray Dalio's call for a 10% to 15% gold allocation is drawing fresh attention, as his Money Rehab comments spread. He prefers gold to crypto as a diversifier, citing US debt risks, while bullion tries to steady after hitting a 14-month low.
The key idea
- The article discusses Ray Dalio's view that investors should always hold 10% to 15% of their portfolio in gold, regardless of market conditions.
- This approach treats gold as a "permanent diversifier," meaning it is held to reduce overall portfolio risk rather than as a short term trade.
- A diversifier is an asset that tends to move in a different direction than other assets in a portfolio, helping to smooth out returns during market ups and downs.
Reader questions
- Why does Ray Dalio prefer gold over crypto as a diversifier? He believes central banks can hold gold, which makes it a more reliable reserve asset, while crypto can be monitored and seized.
- What does Dalio mean by comparing US debt to "plaque building up in arteries"? He is suggesting that rising government debt weakens the financial system, similar to how plaque harms the human body.
- Why is Dalio's advice about "how much" gold to hold, not "when" to buy it? His strategy focuses on long term portfolio structure, suggesting gold should always be part of an investment mix, rather than trying to time market movements.
High-profile endorsements like Dalio's rarely move gold on their own, but they can support retail and wealth-management demand at a time when prices have fallen sharply and some investors are reassessing their allocations. The renewed coverage also coincides with Wednesday's reversal off a 14-month low, which may encourage dip-buyers already watching the $3,500 area. The bigger near-term drivers remain real yields, the dollar and Fed rate expectations, so the long-term case Dalio describes is unlikely to stop short-term swings. For crypto, his skepticism about bitcoin as a reserve asset adds to a debate that matters for long-term institutional demand.

decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] Bank of Korea signals more hikes as 15 of 21 rate projections sit above 3.25%
The Bank of Korea's hike to 3.25% drew two dissents, but board projections lean hawkish: 15 of 21 see rates above 3.25% in six months, 7 at 3.75%. It says inflation will stay above target for a prolonged period and flagged further hikes.
The key idea
- Central banks often signal future interest rate moves through projections, even if current decisions are not unanimous.
- A "hawkish" stance from a central bank means it is inclined to raise interest rates or keep them high to combat inflation. This generally strengthens the local currency and can affect bond yields.
Reader questions
- What does "dissent" mean in this context?
- A dissent means that some members of the central bank's board voted against the majority decision. In this case, two members did not agree with the interest rate hike.
- Why do these projections matter for the Korean won and bond yields?
- Projections of higher interest rates make the Korean won more attractive to investors seeking better returns, which can strengthen it. Higher rates also generally lead to higher short-term government bond yields.
- How do higher interest rates affect different sectors of the stock market?
- Higher interest rates can negatively impact "rate-sensitive" sectors like property and consumer stocks because borrowing becomes more expensive. However, sectors like chipmakers, driven by global demand, may be less affected.
The projections lift the risk that Korean rates peak above the 3.50% most economists expected, which should support the won and keep short-dated Korean government bond yields firm. Two dissents limit the hawkish reading and leave room for the governor's tone to swing sentiment either way. For equities, the higher-for-longer message weighs on rate-sensitive sectors such as property and consumer stocks, while chipmakers remain driven by global AI demand. The bank's focus on household lending also raises the chance of tighter lending rules alongside rate hikes.

South Africa's central bank says AI firms now compete with governments for long-term funding, adding to pressure on borrowing costs. It warns a sharp tech selloff could tighten financial conditions, as AI credit stress builds at CoreWeave and Nvidia.
The key idea
- The rapid growth of AI companies is leading them to borrow heavily, creating competition with governments for long-term funding.
- This increased demand for capital can drive up borrowing costs for everyone, including governments, especially in emerging markets.
- "Credit spreads" refer to the difference in interest rates between a riskier borrower and a less risky one; a widening spread indicates higher perceived risk.
Reader questions
- Why does AI's borrowing affect government bonds? AI companies and governments often tap into the same pool of long-term investors, so increased borrowing by AI firms means more competition for that capital, which can push up interest rates for government bonds.
- What does it mean for emerging markets to be "particularly exposed?" Emerging markets often have higher borrowing costs and rely more on foreign investment, making them more vulnerable to rising global interest rates and capital outflows when investors seek safer assets.
- What are "long-end yields" and why are they important here? Long-end yields refer to the interest rates on long-term bonds, typically those maturing in 10 years or more; they are important because they reflect the cost of long-term borrowing for both companies and governments.
The SARB's warning adds an official voice to a concern that has mostly lived in credit markets until now, and it widens the debate from tech valuations to the cost of government borrowing. The most exposed markets are emerging-market bonds and currencies, which tend to suffer first when global investors cut risk. For equities, the concentration figure is the warning sign: when so much fund exposure sits in a handful of mega-cap names, a selloff in those stocks spreads quickly through portfolios worldwide. Long-end yields and credit spreads on heavily indebted AI borrowers are the gauges to watch alongside the chip stocks.

decisions.headline: Beige Book: Eight of 12 districts report growth as wage pressures pick up
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] Beige Book: Eight of 12 districts report growth as wage pressures pick up
Highlights of the Beige Book released November 25, 2026
- Eight districts reported growth in the slight to moderate range, and four reported no change. In October, nine grew and three were unchanged.
- Consumer spending was little changed as households remained price sensitive and selective.
- Employment rose slightly on balance, with hiring mostly to replace attrition.
- Wages and benefits rose moderately, up from modest in the prior report.
- Prices increased moderately overall, as in the prior period.
- Input cost growth generally outpaced increases in selling prices.
- Most districts expect slight to moderate growth.
The November Beige Book shows an economy grinding sideways rather than deteriorating further, but the inflation story has shifted from prices to wages. Boston slipped to no change from slight growth, joining Chicago, Kansas City and San Francisco in the flat column. Dallas slowed to modest from moderate. Cleveland was the lone upgrade, to moderate growth, on robust manufacturing demand tied to data centers, power generation and defense. Construction declined amid higher borrowing and building costs, and residential real estate weakened.
Wages are the most important change. Wages and benefits rose moderately after modest gains in October, with pressure concentrated in hard-to-fill roles and driven by cost-of-living demands and rising benefit costs. Philadelphia said wage inflation has reached a moderate pace for the first time since 2023, and its contacts expect wage and benefit increases next year at rates last seen in 2023. Dallas reported service-sector wage growth accelerating to an above-average pace. Minneapolis contacts said wages "will certainly have to follow" prices.
On prices, the tone was calmer than October. The national summary no longer tallies robust districts or flags accelerating ones; it simply says prices rose moderately, as before. New York said selling price increases eased slightly, and Minneapolis noted a smaller share of firms reporting higher input costs as fuel prices eased. The pipeline is still full, though. Cleveland reported robust nonlabor cost pressures for a 12th straight period, with one manufacturer planning a 19% contract price increase at the start of the year. Richmond manufacturers' price growth topped 5% for the first time since 2023. St. Louis said many recent cost increases won't hit customers until next quarter. Consumer-facing firms still can't pass costs through, so margins are taking the hit.
The consumer is holding up in aggregate but fraying underneath. Kansas City said spending rose modestly after three straight months of declines, but it also reported workers using earned wage access to pay for workplace meals and households hitting their financial limits on unexpected repairs. Philadelphia retailers saw a late-October lift as gas prices eased and the midterms were resolved, while credit card volumes unusually fell heading into the holidays. Cleveland said food and housing insecurity now reaches middle- to upper-income county employees.
Higher rates are a bigger theme than last time. Dallas cited mortgage rates eclipsing 7%, and its bankers warned that further rate hikes could hurt borrowers' ability to repay. Cleveland bankers said commercial clients are rushing to lock in rates ahead of anticipated increases.
This report is less stagflationary on the price side than October's, but the wage pickup is exactly what the Fed doesn't want to see with inflation already elevated. The FOMC meets Dec. 8-9 and the market is almost fully priced for a hike.
Source URL: https://investinglive.com/central-banks/beige-book-eight-of-12-districts-report-growth-as-wage-pressures-pick-up/

The first place I’d look is the chip stocks. The Nasdaq was down about 4% in morning trading versus roughly 2.5% for the S&P 500. The bounce on Jensen Huang’s return on Monday - orchestrated by the WHite House - gave buyers an opening, and sellers came right back in. The election added to concerns about tighter AI regulation, but with the Jensen Huang allegations, and reinstatement, who can blame the need for more regulation - not the wild, wild west with unlimited uncertainty. [FULL UPDATED ARTICLE TEXT]
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: News] Trump blames the election for the selloff. Here’s what I’m watching.
The Nasdaq fell about 4% in morning trading as the AI selloff deepened, the war with Iran kept oil supply at risk, and fresh tariff proposals added to inflation concerns.
President Trump blamed the November 3 election results for the drop in stocks in a Wednesday post on Truth Social.
The first place I’d look is the chip stocks. The Nasdaq was down about 4% in morning trading versus roughly 2.5% for the S&P 500. Nvidia was down nearly 9% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was off more than 7%. The bounce on Jensen Huang’s return on Monday - orchestrated by the WHite House - gave buyers an opening, and sellers came right back in. The election added to concerns about tighter AI regulation, but with the Jensen Huang allegations, and reinstatement, who can blame the need for more regulation - not the wild, wild west with unlimited uncertainty. When trust goes out the window and we live on the edge of under-regulation, that is a problem.
Then there’s a bigger question for these stocks at current valuations. How much profit will all that AI spending generate, and how long will investors have to wait for it?
The war with Iran is another reason buyers are hesitant despite the recent fall in the price of oil. Iran said two tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. As long as safe passage is in doubt, so is the outlook for oil supplies. Another jump in fuel prices would leave consumers with less to spend and squeeze profit margins. Looking at the price of oil, although it is well off the highs near $120, the price at $83.50 is still well off the levels on February 27 - the Friday before the start of the war. That level was at $67.30. The closing price at the end of 2025 was at $57.40. If $80 is the low, that is still feeding inflation.
Add in fresh tariff proposals from Washington. Why does Pres Trump and company think tariffs are what Americans want especially in times of inflation where corporations are already fighting higher costs. Core PCE inflation rose to 3.3% from 3.1%, and a December Fed hike stays in play.
Then there’s the trust issue in Washington. Can businesses count on the policies they’re making plans around? If you don’t know what your import costs will be in six months, it’s harder to commit to hiring or investment. And if investors have less confidence in what companies will earn, they’ll pay less for those earnings.
Nevertheless, for me, the chip stocks are still the near-term barometer. If it weren't for the AI revolution where would we be. As a result, with stocks at recent lows, that is a concern. Morever, the bounce that we saw on Monday was just into resistance which stalled the rally and led to an equally as fast decline back to the lows on Friday.
The Pres. Trump attempt to push higher was met with a resounding vote of no-confidence.
Source URL: https://investinglive.com/news/trump-blames-the-election-for-the-selloff-here-s-what-i-m-watching/

decisions.headline: ECB and Sveriges Riksbank conclude agreement for Sweden to join T2
decisions.raw_text:
[ECB] ECB and Sveriges Riksbank conclude agreement for Sweden to join T2
- PRESS RELEASE
ECB and Sveriges Riksbank conclude agreement for Sweden to join T2
25 November 2026
- Agreement paves way for settlement of large-value payments in Swedish kronor using T2
- Migration targeted for February 2030
The European Central Bank (ECB) and Sveriges Riksbank have concluded an agreement for Sweden to join T2, the Eurosystem’s real-time gross settlement system. Today, ECB President Christine Lagarde and Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen took part in a signing ceremony for the T2 currency participation agreement at the ECB.
This agreement will enable Sveriges Riksbank to use T2 for settling large-value payments in Swedish kronor. Migration is targeted for February 2030.
Joining T2 will move Sweden’s large-value payment settlement from a national platform to shared European infrastructure. Sveriges Riksbank and Swedish financial institutions will benefit from investments in security, resilience and technological development that are shared across participating markets, as well as from common European standards. Payments will continue to be settled in Swedish kronor using central bank money.
“Shared payment infrastructure strengthens Europe’s strategic autonomy and supports a more integrated financial system,” said ECB President Christine Lagarde. “This agreement builds on our partnership with Sveriges Riksbank and our joint commitment to safe and efficient payments.”
“By connecting to the European T2 platform for settling payments in Swedish kronor, we can, together with the ECB and other central banks, ensure that the Swedish settlement system becomes an even safer and more efficient payment system in the long run, both in everyday life and in a crisis,” said Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen.
TARGET Services are the Eurosystem’s financial market infrastructure for settling large-value payments, instant payments and securities transactions, and for managing collateral. In addition to payments in euro, T2 already supports large-value payments in Danish kroner. Both Sweden and Denmark use TARGET Instant Payment Settlement (TIPS) to settle instant payments in Swedish kronor and Danish kroner respectively.
Photos of the signing ceremony will be available on the ECB’s multimedia portal.
For media queries, please contact Alessandro Speciale, tel.: +49 172 1670791.
Related topics
- TARGET2
- Payment systems
- Instant payments

Please note that related topic tags are currently available for selected content only.
Source URL: https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/pr/date/2026/html/ecb.pr261125_1~6333a90f3a.en.html
