[FULL UPDATED ARTICLE TEXT]
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Commodities] Gold is sitting on the edge of support at $3,425 despite lower yields
The stock selloff is spilling over into gold. A break below $3,425 would give sellers more control, while buyers need to get back above $3,500 to take some of the pressure off.
Gold is trading near $3,441, down about $115 or 3.24%, after reaching a low of $3,426.72. That low came in just above the bottom of a swing area on the daily chart between $3,425 and $3,500. The sellers took the price right to the edge. Can they get through it?
Stocks are getting hit, and gold is getting caught up in the selling
Lower yields would typically help gold. Gold pays no interest, so as Treasury yields move lower, the opportunity cost of holding it falls. Today, the liquidation across markets is taking precedence.
The Nasdaq Composite is down 4.10%, the S&P 500 is down 2.80%, and the Dow is down 1.70% in the snapshot above. When stocks are getting hit that hard, traders raising cash can sell what they own across markets. Gold is getting caught up in that selling today, even as yields move lower.
The $3,425 level defines the risk
For buyers looking for a bounce, the bottom of the swing area gives them a level to lean against with close risk. As long as the price holds above $3,425, they can stay in the game. A break below that level that stays below would give the sellers the go-ahead to probe lower, with the 61.8% retracement at $3,140.67 the next major downside target on the daily chart.
On the topside, the first job for buyers is to get and stay above $3,500. That would put the price back above the swing area and give buyers a technical victory. The next hurdle is the 50% midpoint at $3,610.01. Getting above both levels would do more to dig gold out of its bearish bias.
In the video, I show why the $3,425–$3,500 swing area matters, where buyers can define their risk, and what the price needs to do to give either side more control.
The education. Separate the reason from the risk.
Lower yields can give you a reason to look for a bounce in gold. The chart gives you a place to define your risk. Here, a trader leaning against $3,425 has a nearby level to judge whether the trade is working. If the price breaks and stays below it, the technical reason for leaning against support is gone. If it holds, watch how the price behaves at $3,500. That next test can tell you whether buyers are starting to take back some control.

decisions.headline: Gold is sitting on the edge of support at $3,425 despite lower yields
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Commodities] Gold is sitting on the edge of support at $3,425 despite lower yields
The stock selloff is spilling over into gold. A break below $3,425 would give sellers more control, while buyers need to get back above $3,500 to take some of the pressure off.
Gold is trading near $3,441, down about $115 or 3.24%, after reaching a low of $3,426.72. That low came in just above the bottom of a swing area on the daily chart between $3,425 and $3,500. The sellers took the price right to the edge. Can they get through it?
Stocks are getting hit, and gold is getting caught up in the selling
Lower yields would typically help gold. Gold pays no interest, so as Treasury yields move lower, the opportunity cost of holding it falls. Today, the liquidation across markets is taking precedence.
The Nasdaq Composite is down 4.10%, the S&P 500 is down 2.80%, and the Dow is down 1.70% in the snapshot above. When stocks are getting hit that hard, traders raising cash can sell what they own across markets. Gold is getting caught up in that selling today, even as yields move lower.
The $3,425 level defines the risk
For buyers looking for a bounce, the bottom of the swing area gives them a level to lean against with close risk. As long as the price holds above $3,425, they can stay in the game. A break below that level that stays below would give the sellers the go-ahead to probe lower, with the 61.8% retracement at $3,140.67 the next major downside target on the daily chart.
On the topside, the first job for buyers is to get and stay above $3,500. That would put the price back above the swing area and give buyers a technical victory. The next hurdle is the 50% midpoint at $3,610.01. Getting above both levels would do more to dig gold out of its bearish bias.
In the video, I show why the $3,425–$3,500 swing area matters, where buyers can define their risk, and what the price needs to do to give either side more control.
The education. Separate the reason from the risk.
Lower yields can give you a reason to look for a bounce in gold. The chart gives you a place to define your risk. Here, a trader leaning against $3,425 has a nearby level to judge whether the trade is working. If the price breaks and stays below it, the technical reason for leaning against support is gone. If it holds, watch how the price behaves at $3,500. That next test can tell you whether buyers are starting to take back some control.
Source URL: https://investinglive.com/commodities/gold-is-sitting-on-the-edge-of-support-at-3-425-despite-lower-yields/

decisions.headline: Reader questions — - What durable goods orders measure?
decisions.raw_text:
[REVISION r4 MARGINAL UPDATE (newly added/updated vs r1)]
Reader questions
- What durable goods orders measure?
Durable Goods Orders measure new orders placed with US manufacturers for products expected to last at least three years, such as machinery, vehicles, aircraft and electrical equipment. The indicator provides insight into consumer and business demand, particularly investment intentions, as companies typically order durable goods when they expect sufficient demand to justify expanding or upgrading capacity.
- What does "ex-transport" mean?
"Ex-transport" means excluding transportation equipment orders, which can be very volatile due to large, infrequent purchases like aircraft. Removing them gives a clearer picture of underlying demand.
- Why is non-defense capital goods orders ex-air important?
This specific figure is often seen as a proxy for business investment, as it tracks orders for equipment and machinery that companies use to produce goods and services, excluding defense and aircraft.
- Ex-transport +0.5% vs +0.5% expected
- Ex-defense +0.4% vs +2.3% prior
- Non-defense capital goods orders ex-air +1.2% vs +0.7% expected
US durable goods orders continued to expand in October, giving another positive signal for the manufacturing sector. New orders for manufactured durable goods increased by $0.8 billion, or 0.2%, to $346.7 billion, following September's stronger 2.0% increase.
The headline increase was relatively modest, but the underlying details were more encouraging. Excluding transportation, new orders rose 0.5%, while orders excluding defense increased 0.4%. This suggests that the expansion was not solely driven by volatile transportation or defence-related demand.

decisions.headline: Fed's Williams won't rule out back-to-back rate hikes as data drives the path
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] Fed's Williams won't rule out back-to-back rate hikes as data drives the path
New York Fed's Williams says he is not excluding options and would not rule out rate hikes at consecutive meetings if needed. He has no set timing in mind, says data will lead, and sees tech volatility as no threat to a positive economic outlook.
The key idea
- The Federal Reserve is signaling that it might raise interest rates at consecutive meetings if inflation remains high. This means the pace of rate hikes could accelerate.
- "Back-to-back rate hikes" refers to the Fed increasing its benchmark interest rate at two policy meetings in a row without a pause in between.
Reader questions
- Why does the possibility of back-to-back rate hikes matter for investors? It suggests a more aggressive stance from the Fed, which can lead to higher borrowing costs and potentially slow down economic growth, impacting asset prices.
- What does this mean for Treasury yields and the US dollar? Higher interest rates generally make Treasury bonds more attractive, supporting their yields, and can strengthen the US dollar as investors seek higher returns.
- How does market volatility, especially in tech, factor into the Fed's decisions? According to Williams, only a significant and lasting drop in market confidence that affects spending and hiring would likely make the Fed reconsider its policy.
The openness to consecutive hikes adds upside risk to Fed pricing beyond December, with traders more likely to build in a follow-up move in early 2027. That should keep short-dated Treasury yields supported and give the US dollar a firmer floor, especially against currencies whose central banks are moving toward cuts. For equities, Williams set a high bar for market weakness to change his view, which limits hopes that renewed tech volatility would slow the Fed. Energy remains central to his inflation outlook, so any rise in oil prices would add weight to the case for a faster pace of hikes.
---
Earlier:
- Fed's Williams pins inflation on unusual factors, sees 2027 bringing it lower
- Williams keeps December Fed hike in play as inflation seen above 2% until 2028
---
Williams' message to reporters was simple: December may only be the start, and only a much deeper slide in market confidence than the recent tech sell-off would make him rethink.
Summary:
- New York Fed President John Williams says he would not rule out rate hikes at consecutive meetings if needed
- He says he has no particular timing in mind and has not pencilled in a path, and data will drive decisions

The Philadelphia Fed’s Manufacturing Business Outlook Survey is the oldest of the regional Fed factory surveys, dating to 1968, and one of the most closely watched. It’s released at 8:30 am ET on the third Thursday of the month and covers manufacturers in the Third Federal Reserve District: eastern Pennsylvania, southern New Jersey and Delaware.
The headline is the current general business activity index, which comes from a single question asking firms whether overall activity at their plant increased, decreased or held steady from the previous month. Unlike the Richmond survey, it isn’t a composite of other components. Like the other regional surveys, it’s a diffusion index, calculated as the percentage reporting an increase minus the percentage reporting a decrease, so zero marks the line between expansion and contraction.
The survey also tracks new orders, shipments, unfilled orders, delivery times, inventories, employment, the average workweek, prices paid and prices received. Each comes with a future index for expectations six months ahead. The prices paid index is watched as an early signal of input cost pressures, and the new orders index is a guide to where activity is headed. Most months include special questions on topics such as capital spending plans, wage growth, price expectations or the impact of tariffs.
The sample is relatively small, which makes the headline volatile and prone to large swings that don’t always reflect a change in trend. Even so, the Philly Fed survey tends to move markets more than other regional reports because of its long history and its track record alongside the national ISM manufacturing index.
It’s the second regional survey each month, after the Empire State report. The Philly Fed also publishes a nonmanufacturing survey later in the month.

[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Commodities] NYT: Trump weighs new Iran strikes as Israel presses for a four- to seven-day air campaign
Trump is weighing a new round of extensive strikes on Iran as Israel presses for a joint four- to seven-day air campaign, officials say. No decision has been made, but the report and a fresh tanker attack in Hormuz have pushed oil prices higher.
The key idea
- Geopolitical tensions, like potential military action in the Middle East, directly impact commodity prices, especially oil.
- A "risk premium" is an extra amount added to a price to account for uncertainty or potential negative events. In this case, it's added to oil prices due to the risk of supply disruptions.
Reader questions
- Why does potential military action in the Middle East affect oil prices so much? Military action in key oil-producing regions or shipping lanes, like the Strait of Hormuz, can disrupt the supply of oil, leading to higher prices.
- What does it mean for oil to be "pricing the risk"? This means that traders are factoring in the possibility of future events, such as military strikes or supply disruptions, into the current price of oil.
- How do higher oil prices impact other markets, like gold and currencies? Higher oil prices can fuel inflation concerns, which may lead central banks to raise interest rates, making non-yielding assets like gold less attractive. Oil-importing countries' currencies, like the yen, can weaken as they need to spend more to buy oil.
A renewed US-Israeli air campaign would raise the risk of Iranian retaliation against Gulf shipping and energy infrastructure. With a loaded tanker already hit in the Strait of Hormuz, traders are likely to keep a larger risk premium in crude until Washington’s intentions are clearer. Higher oil feeds straight into the inflation worries that Fed officials raised this week, adding to the case for further US rate hikes. That’s why gold has tended to weaken rather than rally on escalation in this conflict. Oil importers’ currencies, notably the yen, are vulnerable to a further rise in energy costs. Energy stocks stand to benefit.
---

decisions.headline: FOMC Minutes: A couple of participants noted a hike of more than 25 bps could warrant consideration in December
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] FOMC Minutes: A couple of participants noted a hike of more than 25 bps could warrant consideration in December
The minutes of the Oct 27-28 FOMC meeting
It sounds like Waller isn't alone in the 50 basis point hike camp.
- “A couple of participants noted that an increase of more than 25 basis points could warrant consideration at the next meeting if incoming inflation data were unfavorable.”
- A few participants who supported no change in rates suggested it was a close call
- “Some participants” favoured a 25 bp hike at the meeting. Only two members, Cook and Hammack, dissented.
- “Almost all participants” judged that further hikes would likely be appropriate under their baseline outlooks.
- A few of those who wanted to hike said they could have accepted a hold as long as markets clearly understood that more tightening was likely.
- Some participants said market expectations of hikes in December and next year were broadly in line with their own view of the right path.
- The vast majority saw upside risks to inflation, and many called the AI buildout a “material source of inflation risk.”
- A majority noted that financial conditions had tightened since the September meeting.
- Fed staff flagged the risk that inflation expectations could become unanchored after five years of elevated inflation.
The minutes show that the 10-2 vote understated how hawkish this meeting was. In Fed language “some” means more than “a few,” so Cook and Hammack had company among the non-voters. Add the participants who called it a close call and the bloc leaning toward a hike in October was substantial.
This was a conditional hold. Policymakers said outright that market pricing for December was doing part of the work, and several said that alignment was what made it safe to wait. Some of the hawks only accepted a hold because markets were already pricing more hikes.
The most important line is the one about more than 25 bps. A couple of participants said a bigger move could be considered if the inflation data came in unfavorable, and the October CPI did exactly that. Waller set a 0.3% core threshold for 50 bps, and the report met it. These minutes come before that report, so the case for a bigger move has only strengthened since.
The dovish argument rests on financial conditions. Mortgage rates are up, junk spreads have widened sharply, bank shares fell hard, and the market is taking a harder look at AI financing. A couple of officials argued for a gradual approach so households and businesses can adjust. That’s the case for 25 bps in December, but in these minutes it’s the minority view.
The market has 62 bps of hikes priced over the next three meetings, and nothing in these minutes argues against that. If anything, the debate has moved from whether the Fed hikes in December to how much with 27 bps priced in right now and 62 bps at the next three meetings.

decisions.headline: investingLive European news wrap: Risk sentiment remains negative amid rising growth concerns
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: News] investingLive European news wrap: Risk sentiment remains negative amid rising growth concerns
- Market news from the European morning session - 18 November 2026
Articles:
- Zcash extends recovery but significant headwinds persist amid hawkish Fed and US-Iran tensions
- Nasdaq analysis after the much anticipated Nvidia earnings
- Crude oil extends losses despite no changes in the Middle East; demand concerns could be the culprit
- Gold analysis shows we may be in an interesting potential bottom zone
- Bitcoin remains under pressure amid the negative risk sentiment caused by hawkish Fed and US-Iran tensions
- Gold extends losses as strong US dollar and elevated yields hurt. What could change the trend?
- FX option expiries for 18 November 10am New York cut
- What are the main events for today?
- UK October CPI +3.6% vs +3.6% y/y expected
Markets:
- WTI crude oil down -0.89% to $83.95
- Gold down -2.91% to $3,772
- NZD leads, EUR lags
- S&P 500 up +0.32% to 7382
- US 10y Treasury yield down 1 bps to 5.09%
- Bitcoin down -0.23% to $64,153
The main higlight of the session was the UK inflation report. Headline CPI came in line with expectations at 3.6% y/y, while core inflation remained unchanged at 2.8% and services inflation missed forecasts matching last month's 3.7% figure. Although goods inflation accelerated to 3.5%, stable core and softer services inflation provided some reassurance about underlying price pressures. The data led to some minor dovish repricing, with December rate hike odds falling to 78% from 89% before the release.
We also got the final Eurozone CPI report. Headline inflation accelerated to 4.0% y/y in October matching the preliminary estimates, while Core inflation was revised higher to 2.6% vs 2.5% in the flash reading. Energy was the largest contributor to inflation, adding 1.89 percentage points, followed by services at 1.55 percentage points, highlighting persistent price pressures across several components of the economy.
ECB's Vice President Vujcic reiterated that stagflation does not currently look likely, although he expects second-round inflation effects to emerge in 2027. He added that a December rate hike looks very likely under current conditions and considers market pricing for 2027 reasonable. He also stressed that fiscal challenges must be addressed through fiscal policy rather than monetary policy.
Lastly, Fed's Waller doubled down on his hawkish rhetoric saying that US inflation is broadening beyond energy, noting that around 70% of core services components are experiencing inflation above 3%. He warned that businesses may be increasingly willing to pass higher prices on to consumers and argued that the Fed needs to take more aggressive action to bring inflation down, potentially requiring a 50 bps hike immediately rather than signalling a faster tightening pace ahead. He also suggested that the December SEP may offer limited guidance because its year-end projections could fail to capture the evolving inflation picture.
Source URL: https://investinglive.com/news/investinglive-european-news-wrap-risk-sentiment-remains-negative-amid-rising-growth-concerns/
